John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.

Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: The traveller was at the Green Tree, just like you guessed! He gave you a penny for bringing his parcel. You ran right back over the bridge. At the Sauganash, the kitchen had three more errands waiting.
The traveller was at the Green Tree, and he has his parcel back. Then you took a few minutes to watch the drawbridge. The kitchen at the Sauganash noticed! Next time, come straight back.
Wolf Point was the right guess! The traveller was there, and he was glad to get his parcel. You hurried back over the bridge, and all the morning's errands were done before lunch.

The traveller was at Wolf Point, and he has his parcel back. On the way home you stopped to watch the drawbridge, for much longer than you meant to. The kitchen at the Sauganash has been calling you for an hour!

evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.reasoning: The structure record places the tavern at the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, its river end on the bank (position inferred, moved on the owner's ruling T-0141); West Water Street is the west-bank frontage, so the river lies east of it.
evidence.text: The Green Tree's corner is on the west bank of the South Branch, with the river to its east.

evidence.locator: Chicagology, 'Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago': the forks buildings sentence ('partly log and partly frame'), and the note at the page's foot on Wentworth's sign ('He painted a picture of a wolf on it').
evidence.text: Wentworth's tavern at the Point was partly log and partly frame, on the ground north of the Lake Street crossing; Lieutenant Allen made its sign from a piece of a box and painted a picture of a wolf on it.

evidence.locator: DRLOIH, 'The Beginning of Wolf Point', the tavern's operator succession (Walters 1833–1836); DRLOIH hotel chronology, Wolf Point Tavern entry ('ceased operations as a public house in 1834').
evidence.text: One account has William Walters keeping the tavern from 1833 to 1836; the hotel chronology says it ceased operations as a public house in 1834.

evidence.reasoning: DRLOIH puts the tavern 'on the west bank of the river at Wolf Point' and Wau-Bun's 1831 sequence has it 'facing down the river from the west'. That Wolf Point is the confluence is read from the project's committed river trace (the datum origin is the forks), not stated in either sentence. The building's exact distance north of Lake Street is not fixed by any source.
evidence.text: The tavern stood on the west bank at the forks, where the North and South Branches meet and run east to the lake as one river.

evidence.locator: Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1, footnote across pp. 631–632, signed J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble (1883).
evidence.text: Old settlers' statement on the first bridges over the branches: both were built on log abutments and two bents, about ten feet wide, and about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice.

evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12185-12192 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: The bridge across the South Branch near Randolph Street 'at first consisted of floating logs tied together'; Alanson H. and Charles Taylor built it from funds raised by subscription, $486.20, 'of which the Indians of the vicinity contributed $200'.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record's research note holds the conflict open: a floating raft has no abutments, no bents resting on the bottom and no six feet of air beneath it, so four men who used the bridge are preferred over the retold type-word.
evidence.text: Later retellings call the South Branch crossing a log raft bridge; the settlers' statement of abutments, bents and clearance describes a fixed bridge, and the record adopts the fixed reading while keeping the name.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record places the deck at the midpoint of the 69 m reach between Lake and Randolph, between the traced 1834 waterlines; its documented range runs from 1833 to an attestation of 18 August 1835, so it stands on the scene date.
evidence.text: The bridge crossed the South Branch between Lake and Randolph Streets, its west landing on West Water Street; the exact station along that reach is placed at the midpoint because the accounts pull opposite ways.

evidence.locator: p. 87, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 11879-11886 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland call the Sauganash 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its genial landlord, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the bridges section, Norton's letter beginning 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833' and Andreas's correction 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge'; with 'The first drawbridge thrown across the river was at Dearborn Street'. Read in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.
evidence.text: Nelson R. Norton, a ship-carpenter, writes in a letter Andreas prints that he cut the lumber for a drawbridge over the winter of 1833-34 and began building it in March 1834; Andreas notes the Democrat has it formally accepted by the Trustees in August. It was the first drawbridge across the river.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 415 (per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4), the paragraph on the Dearborn Street drawbridge, read verbatim in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.
evidence.text: Andreas: 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' It was of the 'gallows pattern', with frames one at either end of the draw.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record dearborn_street_drawbridge, which places the crossing on the street it is named for and grades the position inferred. The jaunt starts at the south end; the crossing is the route's and claims no dated passage over the draw.
evidence.text: The bridge crosses the main stem in line with Dearborn Street, its south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street.

The errand runner the visitor plays, their age and work at the Sauganash, the traveller, his parcel and his penny, the guess at which tavern he went to, the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Parcel Delivered keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such runner, traveller or parcel is recorded; no named person is met or speaks, and the walk stays on a summer morning of 1835.

opening.text:
JAUNT: A PARCEL ACROSS THE RIVER. It is a summer morning in 1835, and you are thirteen. You run errands for the Sauganash, a tavern by the river. A traveller slept here last night. This morning he went across the river, and he left his parcel behind! He told the kitchen which tavern he was going to, but the kitchen forgot.

Carry the parcel over the bridge and find him. The town, the taverns and the bridge are real. The errand runner is you.

premise: Be the Sauganash tavern's young errand runner on a summer morning in 1835. Carry a forgotten parcel over the river, guess which tavern its owner went to, and pick your way home.

choices.consequence: It is the big tavern right across the bridge.
choices.label: Try the Green Tree

choices.consequence: It is the old tavern up where the rivers meet.
choices.label: Try Wolf Point

stops.narrative: The Green Tree, or Wolf Point?
stops.text: This is the Sauganash, at the corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east side of the river. It is a white building, two floors high, with bright blue shutters. In June the town's newspaper said it had been fixed up, with nice new furniture. The parcel is tied with string, and it is heavier than it looks. Across the river stand two taverns. The traveller went to one of them. Which one?

stops.narrative: The tavern named for a tree.
stops.text: Over the bridge is the Green Tree, at Lake and West Water Streets. James Kinzie built it in 1833. It was the first building in town made to be a hotel. Chester Ingersoll runs it now. It got its name from an oak tree that stood close by. Here is a surprise. This building will still be standing in 1880! Then it will be moved to Milwaukee Avenue. Ask at the door for the traveller. Then go back to the bridge.

stops.narrative: The tavern with a wolf on its sign.
stops.text: This is Wolf Point, on the west side, where two branches of the river meet. The tavern here is partly made of logs and partly made of boards. Its sign was made from a piece of a box. Someone painted a wolf on it! Now, who runs this tavern? Nobody is quite sure. One story says William Walters ran it until 1836. Another says it stopped being a tavern in 1834. Ask at the door for the traveller. Then go back to the bridge.

choices.consequence: There will be more errands waiting.
choices.label: Go back to the Sauganash

choices.consequence: Just a quick look at the town's newest bridge.
choices.label: Go look at the drawbridge

stops.text: You are back on the bridge over the river. It sits between Lake and Randolph Streets. Some old settlers remembered that it stood on logs, about six feet above the water. In winter, wagons could even drive under it on the ice! A later book says it was first made of floating logs tied together. People in town paid for it. The book says "the Indians of the vicinity contributed $200" of the money. Which story is right? The books do not agree. The parcel has found its owner! Go straight home, or take a look at the new drawbridge?

You are back at the Sauganash. One old book calls it the nicest place to stay in the whole town. It says the owner played a happy fiddle and was the best-liked host around. The parcel found its owner. Your hands are empty, and the morning is not even half over. Someone is already calling you from the kitchen!

This is the end of Dearborn Street, where the town's first drawbridge crosses the river. Nelson Norton, a ship builder, cut the wood for it in the winter. He started building it in March 1834. It is about three hundred feet long. The open part, where boats go through, is about sixty feet wide. A frame stands at each end of the part that opens. Watch it for a minute. Then run back to the Sauganash before anyone misses you!
